extracted.intended_audience: Patent practitioners and pharmaceutical/biotech applicants prosecuting or drafting patent applications in India
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether chemical or pharmaceutical derivatives of known substances are patentable in India under Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, including how 'efficacy' is to be understood and what derivative forms are treated as the same substance. Focuses on preventing evergreening and on evidentiary links (e.g., bioavailability → therapeutic efficacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) — new form of a known substance requires enhanced efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance” (text of amended Section 3(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause bars patentability for new forms (derivatives) of known substances unless the new form demonstrably enhances the known efficacy of the substance. The amendment was intended to check repetitive patenting/evergreening while leaving room for 'true and genuine' inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) — new property/use or use of known process restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: “the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or of the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.” (text of Section 3(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newly discovered properties or uses of known substances, or mere use of known processes, are excluded from patentability unless the process creates a new product or uses at least one new reactant. This sets another gate against claiming trivial variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation — what derivatives are treated as the same substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the purposes of this clause, salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of known substance shall be considered to be the same substance, unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.” (statutory Explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute explicitly lists common chemical/pharmaceutical derivative forms and treats them as the same substance by default. To overcome this presumption, an applicant must show the derivative differs significantly in properties specifically regarding efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court interpretation — efficacy means therapeutic efficacy for medicines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that the test of 'efficacy' under Section 3(d) depends on the intended result and, for medicines, 'efficacy' means 'therapeutic efficacy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all advantageous or beneficial properties are relevant — only those directly relating to efficacy (for drugs, therapeutic efficacy). The efficacy test is drug-specific and tied to the product's intended therapeutic result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bioavailability evidence standard — link to therapeutic efficacy required
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase in bioavailability alone is not automatically sufficient; applicants relying on bioavailability must provide evidence establishing that the increase leads to a greater therapeutic efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting patentability on the basis of improved bioavailability, submissions should include data and reasoning that directly connect the pharmacokinetic improvement to a measurable therapeutic benefit (e.g., better clinical outcome, dose reduction with same effect). Mere pharmacokinetic advantages unconnected to therapeutic effect risk rejection under Section 3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy objective — prevent evergreening; require significant efficacy enhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d) was enacted and interpreted to prevent 'evergreening' (repetitive patenting/extension of monopoly) by allowing only derivatives of known substances that demonstrate significantly enhanced efficacy to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy frame distinguishes between impermissible attempts to extend patents through trivial modifications and permissible incremental innovation that yields meaningful therapeutic improvements. Drafting and prosecution strategies should therefore focus on claiming and evidencing genuine efficacy improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) sets a 'second tier' of qualifying standards for chemical/pharmaceutical products
rubrics_metrics.description: As described by the Supreme Court, the amended portion of Section 3(d) 'clearly sets up a second tier of qualifying standards for chemical substances/pharmaceutical products' to admit genuine inventions while checking spurious extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical and pharmaceutical claims, practitioners must meet both the general patentability requirements (e.g., novelty, inventive step where applicable) and the additional Section 3(d)-specific requirement that derivatives show enhanced efficacy where the statute or explanation applies.
